title: The classical algorithm
lead: By default you play against a classical engine without a neural network. It searches the {term:game-tree|game tree} with {term:alpha-beta|alpha-beta}, scores the leaves with a formula whose 13 weights were fitted to game results, and hands over to an exact {term:race-table|race table} once the two armies have passed each other. This page follows one move through all three parts.
sec.board.title: Board and moves
sec.board.p1: The board has 121 cells: a hexagon of 61 cells and six corner triangles of 10 cells each. Each side moves its ten pieces from its own corner into the opposite one. A move is either a step to an empty neighbour cell or a chain of jumps over occupied neighbours, own or foreign. A chain may change direction and may stop after any jump. Nothing is captured. Only the pair (start cell, end cell) counts, so two jump paths to the same cell are one move.
sec.board.p2: In the code, {src:engine/src/main/java/sternhalma/engine/Position.java} keeps one owner byte per cell and a sorted piece list per player. A move is a single `int`, `from | to << 8` ({src:engine/src/main/java/sternhalma/engine/Move.java}). The search plays a move in place with `make` and takes it back with `unmake`, like a command object with `execute` and `undo`. A `Position` is therefore mutable and not thread-safe: every search thread works on its own copy.
sec.board.p3: The move generator finds jump chains with a depth-first search on an explicit stack. A visited set of 128 bits in two `long`s makes sure that each end cell appears once. The order of the generated moves is fixed and pinned by tests, because the search tree depends on it. The start position has 14 legal moves: 6 jumps and 8 steps. The mid-game position used on this page, reached after 30 plies of engine play, has 54.
sec.game-tree.title: The game tree
sec.game-tree.p1: A {term:game-tree|game tree} has positions as nodes and moves as edges. The root is the current position. Its children are the positions after each legal move, their children the positions after each answer, and so on. One level of the tree is one {term:ply}: a move by one side. Depth 4 therefore means two moves for each side.
sec.game-tree.p2: The number of legal moves in a position is its {term:branching-factor|branching factor}. At the start it is 14, and each move again allows 14 answers, so two plies give 14 × 14 = 196 positions. In the mid-game position it is 54, and three plies give about 54³ = {n:157464} leaves. Every further ply multiplies the tree by roughly the branching factor, so no engine sees every position. In the alpha-beta figure with the start position, each of the 14 columns is one move with its 14 answers.
sec.minimax.title: Minimax and negamax
sec.minimax.p1: {term:minimax|Minimax} chooses a move under one assumption: the opponent always answers with the move that is best for them. At the bottom of the tree, an {term:evaluation-function|evaluation function} gives each leaf a score. One level up, the side to move takes its best child. One more level up, the opponent takes the child that is worst for you, and so on up to the root. Minimax visits every node: at depth 2 from the start, that is 14 + 14 × 14 = 210.
sec.minimax.p2: The engine writes this as {term:negamax}. A score always counts from the side to move, so the opponent's best score is the negation of yours, and one recursive function serves both sides: `score = -negamax(child)`. In {src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/AlphaBeta.java} its signature is `negamax(depth, alpha, beta, height)`. Scores are integers. A win `h` plies below the root scores `MATE - h` with `MATE = 1_000_000`, so the engine prefers the shorter win.
sec.alpha-beta.title: Alpha-beta pruning
sec.alpha-beta.p1: {term:alpha-beta|Alpha-beta pruning} returns the same move and score as minimax, but it skips moves that cannot change the result. It passes two bounds down the recursion. Alpha is the score that the side to move is already sure of; beta is the most that the opponent will allow. When a move reaches `alpha >= beta`, the opponent would never let the game get here, so the remaining moves are skipped. This skip is a {term:cut-off}.
sec.alpha-beta.p2: The figure steps through a real search at depth 2 with the evaluator `distance` and no enhancements. By default it shows a position after 24 plies of an engine game, with 67 root moves. The first, H5»N3, sets alpha to −20: the line in the overview. A later move is cut off once one reply holds it at or below alpha, since it can no longer beat the best move; its column stays hollow. Only H5»L6 survives all replies and lifts alpha to −10, the final score.
sec.alpha-beta.p3: Here alpha-beta makes {n:298} calls: 67 at depth 1 and 231 at depth 2, out of {n:3180} nodes in the full depth-2 tree (about 7.3 %). From the start position it makes 55: 14 and 41, out of 210 (about 20 %). The savings depend on the move order. The engine tries replies by distance gain, and with `distance` the first reply is always one of the opponent's best, so every cut-off comes after one reply: the best case. A worse {term:move-ordering|move ordering} searches more. {sec:classical/speedups|Speed-ups} shows the engine's ordering.
sec.budget.title: Strength is a node budget
sec.budget.p1: A {term:node} is one call of `negamax`: the first statement of the function is `nodes++`. Leaves count, the root does not. The check `nodes >= nodeLimit` sits right next to it. A player's strength is its {term:node-budget|node budget}, the number of nodes it may visit per move. The five levels of the app's strength slider are budgets of {n:1000}, {n:5000}, {n:20000} (the default), {n:100000} and {n:500000} nodes ({src:web/src/ui/Panels.tsx}).
sec.budget.p2: A budget in nodes instead of milliseconds makes a game reproducible: the same budget gives the same move on a fast laptop, on a busy server and in every browser engine. To stop at any budget with a usable move, the engine uses {term:iterative-deepening|iterative deepening}: depth 1, then 2, then 3, until the budget runs out. It plays the best move of the deepest finished depth; with the option `partial=1`, which the browser engine sets, it may also use the best move of an unfinished one. Depth 1 always finishes.
sec.budget.p3: In the mid-game position, the browser engine {term:browser-spec|BROWSER_SPEC} completes depth 3 at {n:1000} nodes, 4 at {n:5000}, 6 at {n:20000}, 8 at {n:100000} and 10 at {n:500000}. Without the enhancements, the same evaluator reaches depth 3 at {n:20000} and depth 4 at {n:100000}. The project's notes say: "The evaluation limits strength, not the depth. Four times the nodes was worth +135 Elo. A better evaluation was worth +300 to +500." ({src:docs/search-and-evaluation.md}) {term:elo|Elo} measures a strength difference from match results: +100 Elo means about 64 % of the points ({sec:classical/strength|measuring strength}).
sec.speedups.title: Speed-ups
sec.speedups.p1: A {term:transposition-table|transposition table} stores the result of each searched position: the score, the depth, whether the score is exact or only a bound, and the best move. The same position often appears through different move orders, and the table lets the search reuse the earlier result. Think of a `HashMap<Long, Entry>` with a fixed capacity that overwrites old entries, written as parallel arrays so that no objects are allocated.
sec.speedups.p2: The key is a {term:zobrist-hashing|Zobrist hash}: one random 64-bit number per (player, cell) and one for the side to move, combined by XOR. A move XORs the piece out of its old cell and into its new one, so the hash updates in constant time. The random numbers come from a seeded generator, so the hashes are the same in every run. {term:move-ordering|Move ordering} then searches the table's best move first, then two {term:killer-move|killer moves}, then the moves with the largest distance gain.
sec.speedups.p3: More enhancements come from chess engines: {term:principal-variation-search|principal variation search} (PVS), {term:late-move-reductions|late move reductions} (LMR) and {term:futility-pruning|futility pruning}. Keys of a {term:spec-string|spec string} switch them on ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Strategies.java}). Options that only make a fixed-depth search faster, such as PVS and killer moves, gained nothing at {n:20000} nodes on their own, because every variant still finished depth 4. With LMR and `partial=1`, all options together gained +175 and +143 Elo at equal nodes. Futility pruning raised the mean completed depth from 4.27 to 5.53 plies, worth +139 and +142 Elo at equal cost.
sec.evaluation.title: Evaluation without search
sec.evaluation.p1: An {term:evaluation-function|evaluation function} scores a position without searching further; the search calls it at every leaf. The simplest one, `distance`, counts the steps that each piece needs to reach the goal on an empty board, sums them per side and returns ten times the difference. At the start both sums are 110, so the score is 0. A jump that gains two steps scores +20, a step +10.
sec.evaluation.p2: The engine you play against uses a better function: a weighted sum of 13 {term:feature|features}. A feature is one number that describes the position, always counted as side to move minus opponent. Examples are the summed distance, the distance of the last straggler, pieces already in the goal, pieces still at home, jumps that land closer, and more. Each feature has a {term:weight}. The score is `round(100 × Σ weight × feature)` ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/LinearEvaluator.java}). The figure shows all 13 for the mid-game position: +179.
sec.evaluation.p3: Nobody set the weights by hand. {term:logistic-regression|Logistic regression} fitted them to game results, much like fitting the coefficients of a scoring rule to labelled rows. In the first round these were about {n:68000} positions from {n:2000} engine games, each labelled won or lost. The fit makes the {term:sigmoid} of the weighted sum predict the win probability, so the sum is a {term:logit}: +179 means sigmoid(1.79), about 0.86. On a {term:held-out-set|held-out set} of 400 games, the formula named the winner of 78.8 % of positions, against 76.8 % for distance alone.
sec.race.title: The race table
sec.race.p1: Once every piece of one side stands beyond every piece of the other, the position is {term:passed-position|passed}: no piece can block a foreign piece or jump over one again. The game splits into two one-player puzzles, and the only question left is how many moves each side needs to fill its goal. The engine knows the exact answer from a {term:race-table|race table}, a kind of {term:tablebase}.
sec.race.p2: For every placement of 10 pieces in a region near the goal, the table holds the exact number of moves to fill the goal. {term:retrograde-analysis|Retrograde analysis} builds it as a breadth-first search that runs backwards: start at the filled goal, find all placements one move away, then two, and so on. A {term:ranking-function|ranking function} maps each placement to an array index, so the table stores one byte per placement and no keys ({src:tablebase/src/main/java/sternhalma/tablebase/RetrogradeBuilder.java}, {src:tablebase/src/main/java/sternhalma/tablebase/Ranking.java}).
sec.race.p3: The browser table covers 28 cells: C(28, 10) = {n:13123110} entries of one byte, about {n:13} MB. The server table covers 36 cells: C(36, 10), about {n:254} million entries and {n:254} MB. In a passed position the engine does not search at all. It plays the move whose result has the smallest table count, and outside the table it follows a {term:beam-search|beam search} plan ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/RaceMove.java}). This race play beat the same engine without it by +66.8 ± 16.0 and +58.5 ± 15.5 Elo at equal nodes.
sec.three-players.title: Three players
sec.three-players.p1: With three players, minimax has no single opponent. The engine therefore uses {term:paranoid-search|paranoid search}: the side to move assumes that both others play together against it. The two opponents act as one coalition that minimises its score, the game has two sides again, and alpha-beta works as before ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/ThreePlayerSearch.java}). The score is the mean of the linear evaluation "me against each opponent".
sec.three-players.p2: The three-player spec `BROWSER_3P_SPEC` searches {n:20000} nodes per move and reaches about depth 4. It won 240 of 240 games (100 %) against two random players, which play any legal move, and 112 of 120 games (about 93 %) against two greedy players, which always play the move with the largest distance gain.
sec.strength.title: Measuring strength
sec.strength.p1: The project measures strength in {term:paired-games|paired games} ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Arena.java}). Each pair starts from the same random opening of 4 plies and is played twice with the colours swapped, so neither side profits from a lucky opening. The mean score s becomes an {term:elo|Elo} difference, `400 · log10(s / (1 − s))`, with a 95 % interval: a score of 0.64 is about +100 Elo.
sec.strength.p2: For example, the learned weights of the previous section beat `distance` by +552 ± 89 and +577 ± 96 Elo in two matches at {n:20000} nodes. Later rounds refitted the weights on newer games. {sec:tuning/measuring|Topic 5} explains the method, and {sec:tuning/regression|its section on regression} tells why a better fit does not always play better.
sec.mcts-note.title: What about MCTS?
sec.mcts-note.p1: Many game programs use {term:mcts|Monte Carlo Tree Search}. This code base has it too ({src:search/src/main/java/sternhalma/search/Mcts.java}), but only the network engines use it: the browser engines `net-wasm` and `net-webgpu`, and the self-play of the training. The classical engine never does. The default browser engine is the Java alpha-beta search compiled to WebAssembly GC, with the C++ build as the fallback.
sec.mcts-note.p2: The classical code still serves the network side. Alpha-beta played the teacher games from which the first network learned. The race table and a proven verdict on passed positions ({term:adjudication}) end self-play games early. Random playouts, the classic way to finish an MCTS line, practically never end in this game, so a network takes their place. {sec:inference/why-mcts|The next topic} starts there.

fig.ab.example.label: Example
fig.ab.caption.mid: A real search with the evaluator `distance` and no enhancements, in a position after 24 plies of a game between two engines. Every cut-off here follows after one reply: the engine tries the replies in order of distance gain, and with this evaluator the first reply is always one of the opponent's best. That is the best case for alpha-beta; a worse order would search more replies before each cut-off. Beta stays at +∞: at depth 2 the side to move chooses only at the root, and no choice above the root caps its score. Alpha-beta makes {n:298} calls, {n:67} at depth 1 and {n:231} at depth 2. The full tree of depth 2 has {n:3180} nodes, so alpha-beta visits about 7.3 % of it.

fig.eval.title: Evaluating a mid-game position
fig.eval.desc: A mid-game position after {n:30} plies, and a table of the {n:13} features of the evaluator linear-r3. Each feature counts side to move minus opponent and has a learned weight and a contribution. The contributions add up to the score +{n:179}, a win probability of about {n:86} % for the side to move.
fig.eval.caption: The weights are the set `ROUND3` of the evaluator `linear-r3`, fitted by logistic regression on engine games; the engine's `racelin1-r3` adds race-table arithmetic to it. The score is `round(100 × Σ weight × feature)`, and `sigmoid(score / 100)` is the win probability. A changed weight is only a thought experiment.
fig.eval.board.title: Mid-game position after {n:30} plies
fig.eval.board.desc: The position after {n:30} plies of the engine against itself, with {n:54} legal moves for the side to move. The marks show what the selected feature counts.
fig.eval.table.caption: The {n:13} features, side to move minus opponent
fig.eval.sigmoid.title: Win probability over the score
fig.eval.sigmoid.desc: The curve sigmoid(score / 100), rising from 0 to 1, with a mark at the current score.
fig.eval.overlay.none: Select a feature to see on the board what it counts.
fig.eval.feature.dsum.label: Distance sum
fig.eval.feature.dsum.explain: Steps that all pieces need to the goal on an empty board, summed. Fewer is better, so the weight is negative.
fig.eval.feature.dmax.label: Straggler
fig.eval.feature.dmax.explain: Distance of the piece that is furthest from the goal.
fig.eval.feature.dsq.label: Squared distance
fig.eval.feature.dsq.explain: Sum of the squared distances, divided by 10. It punishes stragglers more softly than the straggler feature.
fig.eval.feature.inGoal.label: In the goal
fig.eval.feature.inGoal.explain: Pieces that already stand in the goal corner.
fig.eval.feature.inStart.label: Still at home
fig.eval.feature.inStart.explain: Pieces that still stand in the start corner.
fig.eval.feature.spread.label: Spread
fig.eval.feature.spread.explain: Distance of the furthest piece minus distance of the nearest piece.
fig.eval.feature.lateral.label: Off centre
fig.eval.feature.lateral.explain: Summed distance of the pieces from the centre line of the board.
fig.eval.feature.jumps.label: Forward jumps
fig.eval.feature.jumps.explain: Single jumps that land closer to the goal.
fig.eval.feature.adjacent.label: Touching pairs
fig.eval.feature.adjacent.explain: Pairs of own pieces on neighbouring cells.
fig.eval.feature.steps.label: Forward steps
fig.eval.feature.steps.explain: Steps to a free neighbouring cell closer to the goal, a measure of mobility.
fig.eval.feature.dsumPhase.label: Race × phase
fig.eval.feature.dsumPhase.explain: The distance-sum difference times the remaining distance of both sides, divided by 100. It lets the weight of the race change as the game goes on.
fig.eval.feature.tempo.label: Tempo
fig.eval.feature.tempo.explain: Always 1 for the side to move: having the move is worth something.
fig.eval.feature.bestGain.label: Best gain
fig.eval.feature.bestGain.explain: Largest distance gain of one move, over steps and jump chains, capped at 6.
fig.budget.title: Node budget and search depth

fig.budget.caption: The five budgets are the levels of the app's strength slider. Only completed iterations count, and wall times are left out because they depend on the machine. In this position the enhancements roughly double the depth at the same budget.
fig.race.title: The race table decides
fig.race.desc: A passed position from a real game: the two sides no longer touch. For each legal move of the side to move, the race table gives the exact number of moves still needed to fill the goal. The engine plays the move with the smallest count.
fig.race.caption: Once the sides are past each other, the browser engine stops searching. It plays the move with the smallest table count; where the table does not cover the placement, a beam search picks the move. Step to the end.
